dossier.public_summary: The dip changes by a factor of more than ten between just three sectors and between individual transits, with two deep events dominating the signal. Imaging cannot place the dip on the target but a nearby star close enough to blend in one TESS pixel can produce it with a normal stellar eclipse. The inconsistent depth best matches a blended eclipse, not a steady transiting planet.

reasons.why: Depth changes by factor >10 between sectors, from 4131 ppm (sector 33) to 56338 ppm (sector 72) and 32730 ppm (sector 87). Tool sector_depths_by_source verdict changes_within_a_source (p_constant_all 1.655850122440653e-38, QLP p_constant 1.9253869966162165e-06) confirms this is not a calibration offset but a real astrophysical change.
Individual transits are highly inconsistent; essentially two deep events out of five drive the entire detection. A planet should have steady depth, not a few outliers at 9 sigma from the mean.
reasons.value: p_consistent 1.4503072866046282e-46, chi2 220.5179992706449 dof 4, share_of_top_3 0.991, outliers 56338 ppm sigma 9.4 and 42246 ppm sigma 8.7 vs 3634 ppm and 4628 ppm

reasons.why: Difference imaging cannot locate the source on-target but finds no clear difference image, and there is a star within one TESS pixel (21 arcsec) that can plausibly produce the dip with a ~14% eclipse. Unstable depth and plausible contaminant together favour a blended eclipsing binary, not a planet on the M dwarf (size rp 4.223 Rearth, Teff 3238 K).
